Patient Vignette: Mark, Age 21

Mark is a slight, serious young man whose posture suggests the weight is carried in his chest. He sits forward in the chair, not relaxed, but poised as if ready to move. He arrives for the session straight from his work at a city-based homeless shelter, where he coordinates intake for families. Married for just over a year, he lives with his wife, Lena, in a small apartment above a laundromat. The smell of detergent, he notes, is a comfort; it reminds him of being clean.

He was nineteen when he joined a faith-based relief organization’s "Call to Serve" program. He had believed, with a bone-deep sincerity, that his faith required his hands to be where the suffering was. Lena supported him, though she was afraid. For five months, Mark worked in a logistics hub near the front line of an active conflict zone. His job was not clinical but practical: unloading trucks of medical supplies, organizing pallets of rice and cooking oil, and helping families navigate the chaos of a distribution point.

The narrative begins at the concrete checkpoint where he worked. He describes mornings in a flat, dusty heat, the sound of generators and the call to prayer mixing with distant thumps he learned to ignore. He became good at ignoring. He learned to look at a man’s shoes, not his eyes, to know if he was a combatant. He learned to parse the tone of a distant explosion: was it outgoing fire (safe) or incoming (not safe)?

The specific event occurred on a Tuesday afternoon. A truck carrying displaced families arrived early, creating a bottleneck. Mark was helping an elderly woman with a child when the ground jumped. The sound was not a bang, he says, but a percussion—a physical blow to the chest. He remembers a hot, metallic taste. He remembers the child in his arms suddenly becoming very heavy. He remembers looking down and seeing a woman’s leg, severed above the knee, wearing a sandal with a single purple flower painted on the strap. He does not remember how he got to the bunker. He does not remember the next four hours.

He was med-evacked two days later for a shrapnel wound to his shoulder. He wears the scar like a brand. He was given a medal by a senior official. He feels nothing about the medal except a deep, cold shame.

Now, at twenty-one, Mark is home. He is working. He is married. He is alive. But he tells me that he is living in a world made of glass. Every loud noise—a car backfiring, a dropped metal tray in the shelter kitchen—sends him into a focused, animal state of high alert. His heart slams against his ribs. He finds himself scanning parking lots for suspicious packages. He avoids crowds, but his job demands them. At the shelter, he has started leaving team meetings to stand in the supply closet, breathing into his hands.

The intimacy of his marriage has become a landscape of fear. Mark cannot bear to have Lena touch his shoulder where the fragment entered. He flinches when she touches him from behind. He has not told her about the sandal. He has not told her about the child. He tells me he feels like an actor in his own life. He watches himself say "I love you," but he feels the words bouncing off a membrane that separates him from everyone. He dreams of sand. He wakes up with his fists clenched.

He drinks coffee to stay alert, but his body is exhausted. His faith, which was once a shelter, now feels like a thundercloud. He cannot pray. He tries, but the words feel like pebbles dropped into a deep well, and he never hears them hit the bottom. He thinks about the woman’s sandal every day. He wonders if her foot was still in it. He has asked God for forgiveness for wondering, which only makes the silence deeper.

His PCL-5 score of 47 reflects what he cannot yet say: that the war did not end when he got on the plane. The war is in his marriage bed, in his church pew, in the smell of diesel from a passing bus. He is a minister still, but he is ministering from behind a thick wall of glass, watching a world he used to inhabit, waiting for a blast that won’t come.
